Albany, March 5—The report of the Lexow Trust
Investigating Committee will be presented to the

that affirmative legislation should be enacted with
a view of restraining it not entirely prohibiting
the operation of such combinations of wealth.

The report states that the committee believes fac-
tor agreements between trusts and their agents
are to great extent the potential agency through
which these combinations are enabled to fulfil the
purpose of their organization.

The committee is working the remedial legisla-
tion, but Chairman Lexow does not think we will
have the bills ready for introduction tomorrow.
One of them to be introduced by the committee
will be that prepared by Attorney General Hancock
last year aimed especially at the Coal trust

appointed by him, he shall get authority to pro-
ceed against trusts from the Supreme Court. An
other amendment will provide that the testimony
obtained from witness against trusts shall not
be used in any criminal proceeding and that a wit-
ness shall have absolute immunity from prosecution.

The committee is considering preparation of

report far they refer to the Sugar Trust. In

the American Sugar Refining Company has pre-

organization of the company the price of sugar
has been lowered to the consumer, labor has been
kept steadily employed and to a greater extent

has not solicited the cooperation of any factors

sounds were heard. All the spectators

communion of bread and wine was ob-
served. Then came the observance of the
last supper. Baskets of plates and forks
and spoons and knives were brought in
and arranged on the table. Then came
dishes of cold staple foods, such as roast
beef, pork and beans, bread and water.

and one heard only the rattle of knives
and forks. Each person had been ex-
horted to remember the meaning of the
supper.

Lord's last supper, the Dunkards rose to
their feet at given signal and with
bowed heads sang two verses of a sacred
hymn and went out of the hall and home
without another word escaping their lips.
At home the greater part of them re-
mained in silent prayer all last night.

A matriculate at a certain Cincinnati
medical college is introduced to the mu-
scum by committee of students before he
Is allowed to visit the rest Of the institu-
ton. This museum is probably the most
wonderful of its kind in existence, and
contains among other things of more or
less interest the gold jointed skeleton of a
man seated on chair with pipe between
his teeth, looking down into freshly dug
grave.


There is an interesting story connected
with this old mans bones, and they are
deeply reverenced by the college faculty.


A good many years ago there was in the
employ of the college a resurrectionist,
nicknamed "Skel'' by the students, whose
business it was to supply the college with
dissecting material sufficient for the pur-
suance of the study of anatomy by the stu
dents. "Skel' had in consequence quite
an unenviable reputation as grave rob-
Der and was held in great fear by the me-
groes and ignorant country people. He
was well liked by both faculty and stu
dents, however, as he always contrived in
one manner or another to keep the stu
dents well supplied with "stiffs" during
the dissecting season, and grew from IA
young into an old man, and finally died
In the service of the college.


But before he shook off this mortal coil
he willed that when he died his body
should be dissected by the students of the
college he had served so long and faithful
ly. His remains were finally disposed of
according to his wish, and at a meeting of
the faculty it was decided to honor his
bones by mounting them in gold joints
and placing them in the museum of the
college, with his old corncob pipe between
his teeth, sitting on "a chair, his head bent
down and resting on the handle of spade,
gazing intently at a freshly dug grave with
the newly upturned earth on the side,
which the students each year decorated
with beautiful floral piece emblematic
of the occasion. st. Louis Republic

An affair of importance called Mr. Baker to Philadelphia last Thursday, already noted. In the course of his business dealings that day he received a check running into four figures which was not made payable to his order. The check was drawn by a Philadelphia house of high commercial standing on one of the most prominent banks in the city. After receiving the check it occurred to Mr. Baker to have it certified so he called at the bank and went to the paying-teller's window.
"Twill you kindly certify this?" he requested.
The teller, a gentleman perhaps sixty years old, who looked as if he had spent half a century in the banking business, politely returned the check to Mr. Baker, and said: "I cannot certify this without the permission of the drawer of the check or at his request."
Mr. Baker was almost dazed for a second, but immediately asked why not?
"A rule of the banks prevents me, sir," replied the teller.

"Well," said Mr. Baker, "this is a brand-new experience for me—of course, don't want you to break a rule. There must be an excellent reason for such a rule. In my pursuit of knowledge, will you kindly inform me why that rule is in force? But my business experience has taught me that I am not demanding anything unusual in asking certification on a check drawn by one of your depositors. Surely I have the right to know that this check is good."
"Oh, my, sir, the check is good. It is drawn by one of our largest depositors," hurriedly answered the teller.

"That may be, my friend," suavely remarked Mr. Baker. "You assure me that the check is good, you ought to know, and consequently believe you. But the next man I pass this check to may not have the same confidence in my certification as I have in yours."
"Why, I couldn't certify this check anyway," answered the teller. "I haven't the authority, and besides, if I did, I'd have to charge it up right away to the account on which it is drawn."
"Wh-wh-why, certainly you would," said Mr. Baker, gasping in amazement, "that's just what I supposed you'd do."

"But suppose there are other checks on this account? I couldn't give yours the preference over them."

While Mr. Baker was trying to intelligently digest this line of argument the teller remarked that he would see the president of the bank and ask him if he would break the rule and allow the check to be certified. After a whispered consultation the teller returned to Mr. Baker and announced that he had secured permission to break the rule and certify the check which he proceeded to do.

"Imagine the business of Wall Street being carried under such banking rules," observed Mr. Baker to a friend to whom he related his experience. "And understand that the rule the teller quoted to me is observed by all the Philadelphia banks. Phew!"

Perhaps visions of an angry bear defending her cubs cooled the ardor of the hunting party, but why it was thus no man telleth. For several days afterward our streets were reminder of old colonial times when every man carried a gun at his side. It is forcible illustration of how history repeats itself as the oldest inhabitants tell the story that some 80 years ago bear was seen at the foot of Steward hill on Main street. Then as now men and boys started in pursuit, but of no avail, for the bear stayed under an old barn until all danger was past and escaped unframed. It is said in this case of last Wednesday that the next morning the old bear was seen near the shore of the river where she crossed with her cubs the day before. Perchance she came back for the purpose of taking in the town, thinking it favorable and safe place for winter quarters.

WASHINGTON, March 3—The president
has sent to the senate a report made by
secretary Olney on the resolution request-
ing the correspondence in the case of DR.
Ricardo Ruiz. The report suggests the in-
advisability of supplying the correspond-
ence, at this time, which suggestion the
secretary endorses, saying that it would
be incompatible with the public interest
to do so pending the public and exhaustive
INVESTIGATION about the case instituted.

The president adds the suggestion that
the consul general should have professional
aid in such investigation, though that
matter, together with the selection of in
particular PERSONS TO act with him, properly
 devolves upon my successor in office.

Instead of transmitting the official cor-
respondence the secretary supplies an ac-
count of his own COMPOSITION covering the
essential facts in the case. He says that
Ruiz, a native of Cuba, came to this coun-
try during the revolution which termi-
nated in 1873 and studied dentistry in
Philadelphia, declaring his intention to
be a citizen of the United States in
1877. He received his final papers in 1850.
After this he returned to Cuba and has
resided there since. He details Ruiz's ar-
rest on Feb. 4, of which he says the depart-
ment was immediately informed, but that
nothing more was heard in regard to the
matter until Feb. 2, when the consul
general reported that Ruiz had been found
dead. He says the department had as-
sumed that the case was being attended to
during this interim and that a demand
would be made that the prisoner should be
put in comunicado but that it afterward
developed that no such demand had been
made, and the prisoner had remained con-
stantly in solitary confinement. The cir-
cumstances attending the death were such
as to lead to "A demand for immediate in-
vestigation."

Consul General Lee's Report.

After such personal examination as he
was able to make, the secretary continues, "The consul general has reported to
the department that Ruiz was placed and
kept for 50 hours in a small, closed and
filthy cell 6 feet by 3, having a rough stone
floor with no window, and only one
square opening in his door for the admis-
sion of air, which aperture was kept shut
so tight when so used that no one was al-
lowed to see him; but he died from neg-
lect or violence; that he became deranged;
that an autopsy showed seven contusions
on top of the head; that he died from con-
gestion of the brain; that there was no
fracture of the skull, but that an knowl-
edge was confined to officials, and that it
was difficult to ascertain the facts.

He says that, on the other hand, B.
Ditt. governor general of Cuba, in a re-
port made to his government on Feb. 9,
states that Ruiz was confined in a room
8 feet by 10, with a large window,
that the room showed no sign of damp-
ness; that Ruiz had an easy chair and
comfortable bed. This official also reports
that Ruiz was found in his room ver-
y much excited, with "a confusion on his
head," after a blow was heard in the room.
He says the prisoner was then removed to
a better room; that on the 9th he was
found by the attendant in the act of hurt-
ing his head against the grating of his
door and, though quieted by the attend-
ant shortly after, died.

The conclusion of the official reports of
the two governments being thus RADICAL,
conflicting, the secretary says another
open and thorough investigation seems to
the government indispensable and the
Spanish government concurred in this
view.

The secretary incloses a copy of Minis-
ter de Lome's letter acceding to this re-
quest. He says that Ruiz did not make
known his American citizenship when
arrested, a circumstance which, he says,
often occurs and always leads to complica-
tions.

London Times.


The following letter to the London
Times tells a rather interesting experience and is good illustration of the
way Englishmen write to that paper
about all sorts of topics:


To the Editor of The Times


SIR,—A curious parallel to your correspondence Mr. Wycliffe's exorcism of the ghost that
haunted the house at Oxford occurred some few
years ago in an old Oxfordshire mansion, of
which friends of my own had recently become
possessed soon after the new owner's arrival.
The strange discovery was made that on the
upper floor containing the servants' apart-
ments and the children's nurseries, there was
a chamber which had long been known as
haunted and in which no one could ever be in-
duced to sleep. By daylight it was a pleasant,
sunny room, but to be in it at night, so every
occupant declared, was enough to chill the very
marrow in one's bones. No sooner was the
house all quiet, doors and windows shut and
midnight near, ringing from the church tower,
then strange sounds, heard nowhere else, be-
gan to fill the haunted room. Weird music
broke the silence, now sweet and soft and love-
ly as dream, then swelling into wild confu-
sion, then dying away in long drawn moans of
infinite distress. Nothing was ever seen, but
there was no delusion as to the sounds. It was
no use putting in a new servant, ignorant of the
secret known. The noise, as of a
soul in pain, so it was steadily affirmed, pro-
ceeded from no human visitation. The room
was haunted and it was not to be expected
that one would sleep in company with a
ghost.


My friend, the mistress of the house, was a
woman of great nerve and common sense. She
needed the room for household use and she
resolved to lay the ghost. Accordingly she had
made ready for occupation and after a care-
ful examination of everything in the apartment prepared to spend the night in it herself.
The tales were quite true. Toward midnight
when all was still the ghostly music began to
quiver through the silence, sweet and wild and
exquisitely sad. My friend listened, not quite
guilty, perhaps, of tremulousness. Then she rose
and examined the room carefully afresh. Presently it struck her that the sounds proceeded
from one corner of the floor. She lifted the
rug, put her ear down and found it to be the
case. She had located the ghost, if it was not
laid. Next morning carpenter was sent for;
the boards were taken up and immediately
beneath there was revealed a perfect plexus of
bell wires, which had been conducted by the
route to different parts of the house. When
doors and windows were all closed and every-
thing still at night, the wind, finding its way
by what channel it could, turned this la-
byrinth of wires into an organ harp, whence
issued the mysterious sounds by which successive households had been scared. The wires
were adjusted, the chinks and crannies closed
up, the ghost was laid and the haunted room
has been comfortably occupied ever since.

SAN FRANCISCO. March 12.—The Pacific Mail and the Occidental & Oriental Steamship Companies, together with the Southern Pacific Company, are much concerned over the decreasing volume of trade entering the port of San Francisco from the Orient.

There was a conference between the officials of the lines mentioned in the office of Mr. Smurr, general freight agent of the Southern Pacific Company, Thursday afternoon, at which the traffic situation was discussed at considerable length, and various proposed measures for its improvement discussed. No decisive action was taken, however.

"The trouble lies in the fact that there is not enough east-bound business for all the lines now plying to and from the Orient," said Mr. Smurr, in discussing the matter, "but decided for the present to do no more than we have been doing of late in the direction of fighting for the business, viz: the making of rates in competition with the rates via other lines and via the Suez route.

As matters now stand, rates fluctuate with the departure of every steamer. Our representatives at Yokohama are compelled to make rates to meet the rates offered by the other lines, and we never know what the rates are until the steamer arrives here. That does not evince a very healthy condition of affairs, but we have not as yet discovered any means of improving matters."

Mr. Smurr said that the new Japanese steamship line, the Nippon Yusen Kaisha, which connects with the Great Northern railway at Seattle, was getting its share of the east-bound freight traffic, a part of which, at least, would otherwise come to San Francisco; he was inclined to think, however, that the Nippon Yusen Kaisha was more of competitor of the Suez route than of lines plying between Japan and this Coast.

It is generally admitted, nevertheless, that the new line to Puget Sound has proved a disturbing factor of considerable consequence, and that the existing instability of rates is largely due to the increased competition afforded by its steamers.

The competition for freight traffic, originating in the Orient, has never been more keen than at present. It has caused a serious disturbance in rates, and the Pacific Mail and the Occidental & Oriental Steamships foresee no means at present for improving matters.

NEW YORK, N. Y., Oct. 16.—The popular reception to Miss Evangelina Cisneros in Madison-square Garden to-day was an extraordinary demonstration. Fully some 600 people, nearly one-third of them well-dressed women, crowded the upper half of Madison-square Park and filled Broadway and Fifth avenue, and waited patiently for the congratulatory speeches to be finished and the Cuban heroine to appear.

A stand has been erected north of the Worth monument, from which the speech was delivered, and on which the Seventh Regiment Band was stationed. The crowd began to grow little restless, and it was decided at 9 O'Clock that the young lady must be brought on. J. Lincoln de Zayas was speaking when carriage containing Miss Cisneros and Karl Decker, her rescuer, appeared at the stand.

For some moments the two stood forth while the cheering continued. Then Miss Cisneros was led back to the rear of the platform, where she bowed and smiled to the crowd on that side of the platform. Then she ascended the steps to the carriage, which was driven around the square and back to Delmonico's.

Previous to the appearance of Miss Cisneros on the platform there were a number of short speeches, interspersed with selections by the band. Murat Halstead was chairman, and introduced the speakers. United States Senator Thurston of Nebraska was the first speaker. He was very coarse and could be heard for only a few feet from the stand.

Mr. Thurston said that it was the duty of our government to grant belligerency to the Cubans. "If I had my way," said he, "not only would the belligerency of Cuba be recognized but I would send a battleship to anchor in Havana harbor in order to inspire with hope and courage those who are struggling for freedom."

murder theory the explanation is made of
the marks on the hand that the holes were made
by insects eating through the flesh and that
the long marks are the natural lines of the
hand made more distinct by the contraction
of the flesh. The contraction of the muscles
and tendons it is said, would also cause the
cramped condition of the fingers. The au-
thorities are divided between the two op-
tions. Within few feet of where the missing
hand was found the stocking which had
covered the dead girl's right foot and leg was
also discovered. What is believed to be a
significant fact relative to the time the body
lay on the hillside developed with the finding
of the hand and stocking. Both lay on top
of rather than under the dead leaves. Some
leaves that have left the trees this fall were
sparsely scattered about the hand and stock-
ing, but only a few of them were on the
articles and did not hide them from view.

According to Mr. Morisette, who is an ex-
perienced woodsman, the hand and stocking
were on top of last year's fall of leaves. If
his judgment is not at fault this would seem
to indicate that the body was deposited on
the hillside after last winter's snow left
the ground and corroborates the original theory
that it had only been exposed to the weather
since, perhaps the early months of the past
summer. This theory is also substantiated
by the condition of the dead woman's cloth-
ing, which is in a state of excellent preserva-
tion. It is rotted in some places where it
had been pressed against the ground by the
weight of the body, but otherwise the cloth
is only slightly soiled and strong of texture.

On the other hand from the fact that the
body was left on the hillside, where it did not
stand in water and was very little exposed to
the rays of the sun, it is believed by some
physicians, interested in the case, that it
may have been where it was found for more
than a year. If it was placed on the hill
previous to last winter it is said that the
body would have been frozen early in the
fall and thus no decomposition would have
taken place until it thawed out the following
spring.

The theory of self-destruction was suggested
by the finding of the broken glass, but the
idea of suicide is not strong in the minds of
the investigating officials, as it is said if the
woman had taken poison she would have
drunk it from the bottle. That any one would
have carried a delicate glass to the lonely
spot is considered very improbable. In fact
the presence of the glass on the hillside is
held to be no easier to account for than the
disposal of the body. The unusual
condition of the three pins is also a subject
of much speculation. They were found on the
identical spot where the body had been
thrown. If the body was exposed any length
of time, and the condition of the skeleton
shows at least some months' effects of the
elements, the only explanation for the cond-
ition of the pins is that they were secured
from the dampness by being closely wrapped
somewhere in the dead girl's clothes. No
trace of hat or wrap of any kind could be
found, nor could the search of the entire
party discover the missing shoe. The shoe
already found is low pattern of No. 4 size
and little worn. After the exhaustive search
the dead leaves on the hillside were set a-
fire and a considerable area burned off. If the
supposed murder was committed near where
the body lay it was thought likely that some
kind of a weapon, either a knife or a re-
volver might be hidden beneath the leaves,
but no weapon of any kind was disclosed
when the ashes were raked, after the fire died
out. All of the articles found by the search-
ing party were taken in charge by Assistant
County Attorney Zolman, who expressed
himself as more firmly than ever convinced
that the unknown girl had been murdered.

Then it comes to pass, when the moment of keenest agony is reached, that the starving man begins to eye his companion with the wolf glare of a beast of prey. His pangs become paroxysmal. During their greatest intensity there springs up within him fierce impulse to slay his neighbor that he may feed on his flesh and slake his thirst with his blood. This terrible prompting to cannibalism, it may be noted, is, however, rare except in cases of famine from shipwreck.

Although it is customary to regard it as common feature of starvation and to make thrilling statements of the frequency with which even mothers will, under the goad of hunger, kill and eat their children, and though startling assertions to this effect have been made by historians of great sieges, yet it ought to be said that as general rule, well authenticated cases of cannibalism among civilized people will be found to occur only at sea. They are very rarely found on land. And, what is more curious still, whenever famished, shipwrecked men set foot on shore, no matter how desolate and barren may be their rock of refuge, they seem as by magic at once to banish from their minds the very idea of anthropophagy, or man eating, and that, too, though they might have been resignedly contemplating it as an imperative necessity few hours before.

In the case of Ensign Prenties of the Eighty-fourth regiment and his companions, who were wrecked on the barren island off Cape Breton in 1880, the difference between famine on shore and on sea is curiously exemplified. Prenties records that they were able to endure the most fearful pangs of hunger without ever so much as thought of resorting to cannibalism for relief, so long, however, and only so long, as they kept on land. But when they took to their boats—and it was not once merely that they experienced this—in order to escape from their rock bound prison, though they were not a whit worse off for food than they were on land, yet the moment they put to sea with one accord they began to think of killing and eating one of their number. On the other hand, when they found their attempt to escape futile and put back to shore, whenever they landed the horrible idea of cannibalism seemed to vanish. — Science For All

All of the killed and injured resided

The explosion came just as three cars
were almost in the center of the space
at the corner. The first one was on its
way directly across Tremont street on
Boylston; the second was just turning
from Tremont to Boylston, while the
third was close behind this one. There
was another car on Boylston waiting for
an opportunity to turn into Tremont, and
behind this were several others.

The first-named car was precisely in
the center when the explosion came. The
whole of the wooden work, which is
used as a bridge over the deep hole at
this point, was lifted with a frightful
roar, into the air, carrying the first
named car with it, and taking along the
two horses of the second car. The other
vehicles were lifted into the air.

Instantly the air was filled with flying
debris, and above the shouts of terror,
stricken pedestrians could be heard the
groans and cries of the wounded. The
first electric car, the one in which most
of the people were killed, fell back upon
the tracks and broke in halves. The por-
tions immediately broke into flames. Then
someone sounded fire alarm and calls
for the ambulances.

Within few minutes the Emergency
Hospital ambulance was on the scene.
Other ambulances followed and the fire
department responded promptly and ex-
tinguished the flames. A squad of 100
policemen was insufficient to keep back
the thousands of people who rushed in
from all sides, and it was only by giving
a false alarm of second explosion they
were able to drive back the crowds and
rope off the street.

The firemen, police, and laborers con-
veyed the dead to the morgue and the
injured to the hospitals.

Not only were all the window fronts
broken in the neighborhood, but from Jew-
eler's window precious stones, said to be
worth $4,000, were scattered about the
street. The foundations of the Hotel Pei-
ham are said to have been shaken badly,
while every window display in the neigh-
borhood was injured more or less. It is
utterly impossible to estimate the loss in
that direction.

The immediate cause of the explosion is
of course uncertain, but the most generally
accepted theory is that it was started by
a spark from the electric motor of the
Mount Auburn car igniting the gas which
escaped from the old main that runs along
the south side of Boylston street.

The laws of the state require that all
children between the ages of six and
fourteen years shall attend school a
certain number of weeks each year;
and this requirement of the law is
pretty generally complied with, as all
feel that it is a wise one Now, many
children complete the eight grades of
the public schools before they are
thirteen years old; last spring one lit
tie girl completed all the grades quite
while before she was twelve. There
are children who finish the grades be-
fore they have attained the school age
limit to go to school if the high school
is abolished. Even if it is suggested
that they so to the preparatory depart
ment of the university, which some
seem to think is an omnium- gatherum,
| this will be found impracticable, be-
cause it is not deemed advisable by the
university authorities to admit any one
there under the age Of fourteen. If the
children who come from the grade
schools before they are fourteen can
not go to a high school, where shall
they go? The law says they must go
to school. but if there is no school to
| go to. what is to be done? 1t may be
answered that they can be sent to pri-
vate schools, but that is not what the
law contemplates, though the option of
sending children to a private school
exists. But the cost of sending a child
to a private school will far exceed the
amount of taxes that the parent would
have to pay as his proportion for the
support of the high school


The requirement of the law that
children shall attend school until they
have reached a certain age puts a new
phase on this high school question, one
that has escaped notice.

owing to the Sailors union fixing the
wages of sailors at $50 a month and
engineers and other ship employees at
about twice the wages paid by Euro-
pean steamers, it would be impossible
for us to compete with the English,
German, Italian and Scandinavian
ships already on the Pacific ocean.

After the war with China, the Jap
anese appropriated a large amount of
their war indemnity for a subsidy to
their merchant marine, and we opened
negotiations with the General Steam
ship company of Japan, which is owned
by the leading men of the empire. We
found their subsidy was about equal
to the cost of their coal and the wages
of their sailors. They pay their sail
ors $15 a month, Mexican, or $3.50 in
gold, enabling them to hire twelve good
sailors for the wages of one American
sailor. After some protracted and diff-
icult negotiations we concluded a con-
tract with them for a line of steamers
between Chinese and Japanese ports
and Seattle, on condition that they
would carry flour from Puget Sound to
the Asiatic ports at 50 per ton, against
81 to 15 per ton formerly charged from
west coast ports in the United States.
This low rate fixed the rate for all
other lines between the Pacific coast
and Asia and has resulted in carrying
about 2,600,600 bushels or its equivalent
in flour from the last crop. There is
left, understand, about 1,000,900 bush
els to be moved between now and next
harvest.

Thus you will see we have been able
to find new mouths which have never
before used wheaten bread to take the
entire California, Oregon and Washing-
ton wheat crop out of the European
markets. This will reduce the amount
going to Europe about 20 per cent and
in bushels about 10,900, three times
the quantity shipped to Europe from
the Argentine during the past crop year.
The prices of wheat this year as com-
pared with last, are about 20 to 15 cents
higher, and I think it may be said that
from 15 to 15 cents of this rise is clear-
ly due to the withdrawal of all Pacific
wheat from the European markets. I
see in this morning's market reports
a telegram that European ships are
loading with barley, rye and merchan-
dise from San Francisco to Europe, af-
ter waiting four months for cargoes of
wheat, and that no more wheat will go
to Europe from the Pacific coast. The
only way we could bring about this
great reduction in the cost of transpor-
tation of flour to Asia was by diverting
the tea and mating business which has
heretofore gone mainly on English ships
from Asia direct to New York and
bringing those commodities to the Pa-
cific coast by a low rate of transporta-
tion inland by rail to distribute the
commodities to points between San
Francisco and New York.

I have given you the details so that
you will understand the situation and
be able to see that unless these ships
can bring their main cargoes of mer-
chandise to Pacific ports at rates that
will compensate them for the traffic,
the business must go as heretofore, to
New York, and the rates on our to
Asiatic ports will be again at the old
figure, or an advance of about 50 cents
a barrel which would, in my judgment
destroy the business that has just be-
gun to be built up with that country.
The province of Anhui alone, which is
near the coast, contains over 50,600,900
of people, and at 20 pounds of flour per
capita per annum, would consume the
product of 10,900,900 bushels of wheat.
The large districts of Tien Tsin and
Shanghai, both easily accessible from
the sea, would consume about as much
more as soon as the trade can be fully
opened.

It is not outside the range of posi-
bility that we could ship wheat from
Devils Lake to the Pacific coast for
this trade. We certainly could at 50
cents a bushel cost for the wheat at
Devils Lake or points west as long as
the demand for flour continues to grow
as it has for the past six months."

Minister Thurston, General W. S.
Smith and Judge Hartwell—now here
at work. They favor the incorpora-
tion of territory under the strong
protection of this Government. Their
expressed belief is that there is a
sufficient Anglo Saxon population on
the island to guarantee a stable Re-
public, else they would not be in favor
of any change from existing condi-
tions.

met with encouragement since they
got to work. There is strong feeling
in the House, led by New England
members principally, and in the Sen-

spirit by the Administration, and
while they are desirous of securing
action at as early day as practicable

ministration to first dispose of the
tariff, and will not unduly press the
Hawaiian question.

be considered at this special session
but failure to secure action at this
session will not be by any means con-
strued by them as a defeat or discour-
agement. It is believed a majority of
the Foreign Affairs Committee is in
favor of such action. Thurston said
tonight that he was very much pleas-
ed with the status of affairs at the pres-
ent time. He seemed to have no rea-
son to fear other than favorable ac-
tion.

In The Century General Horace Porter
IN Campaigning With Grant relates the
following anecdote Of Grant:


Earthworks had been thrown across the
neck of land upon which City Point is lo-
cated. This entrenched line ran from a
point on the James to a point on the Ap-
pomattox river. A small garrison had been
detailed for its defense, and the command
ing officer wishing to do something that
would afford the general in chief special
delight, arranged to send the band over to
the headquarters camp to play for him
while he was dining. The garrison com
mander was in blissful ignorance of the
fact that to the general the appreciation of
music was a lacking sense and to him a score was a sealed book.


About the third evening after the band
had begun its performance the general,
while sitting at the mess table, remarked,
"I've noticed that that band always begins
its noise just about the time I am sitting
down to dinner and want to talk. I
offered to go and make an effort to sup
press it, and see whether it would obey an
order to cease firing," and my services
were promptly accepted. The men were
gorgeously uniformed, and the band
seemed to embrace every sort of brass in
instrument ever invented, from diminutive
cornet-a-piston to a gigantic double bass
horn. The performer who played the lat
ter instrument was engaged within its
ample twists and looked like a man stand
ing inside the coils of a whisky still. The
broad belted bandmaster was putting with
all the vigor of quack medicine adver-
tisement, his eyes were riveted upon the
music, and it was not an easy task to at
tract his attention. Like a sperm whale,
he had come up to blow, and was not go
ing to be put down till he had finished.
But finally he was made to understand
that, like the hand organ man, he was de
sired to move on. With a look of disin-
heritance on his countenance, he at last
marched off his band to its camp.


On my return the general said: "I fear
that bandmaster's feelings have been hurt.
I didn't want him to be wasting his
time upon a person who has no ear for
music." — A staff officer remarked, "Well,

day he came to take command of his es

sent for the executive officer and said to

that band thrown overboard at once!'"

Governor Powers of Maine in his
inaugural address congratulates the
people of his state on the fact that the
young men have very generally ceased to
go to the far west to carve out fame and
fortune for themselves. The same
forces, however, that operated in the
past to draw to the west the ambitious
youth of New England still exist even
though partially latent, and must soon
exercise their full influence again. So
long as the west is still to be developed
and offers better opportunities for young
men to rise in life the temptation to
migrate must continue. 1t will be many
years yet until the country is so evenly
populated and its wealth so generally
distributed that the movement from east
to west shall cease to be appreciable.

As a tribute to the memory of its late Commander Admiral Richard W. Meade, Lafayette Post No. 140 has ordered, by resolution, that the Office shall remain vacant for three months from May 2. The vacant chair, the altar and the colors will be suitably draped and officers will wear the emblem of mourning on their sword hilts during the same period. Senior Vice and Acting Commander Josiah G. Long and Adjutant Wilbur H. Brown, in special order No. 2, thusly commemorate the virtues of so worthy representative of the order to which the post proudly belongs. He was a man, it says, "of rare nobility and simplicity of character of the Grand Army of the Republic, and the utter devotion of a rare gentleman, and his life has served the Navy of his country; and the pages of history where will be recorded the deeds of those who have lived and his life's course honor and courage, an innate feature of his soul, and his name is in sorrow but the eloquence of such a name shall be his monument; we treasure his memory and dwell upon his companionship."

Colonel Joseph A. Goulden, first vice-chairman of the New-York Memorial Committee, is now acting chairman of the committee, in the absence of Governor Horace Porter, Ambassador to France. The acting chairman appreciates the importance of teaching the rising generation lessons of patriotism, believing that without such teaching the education of the schools is imperfect. He wants to form a small corps of comrades who can be depended upon to make short addresses to the schoolchildren on patriotic subjects. He has, therefore, with the concurrence of Secretary Atkinson, sent circular letter to the commanders of all the Grand Army posts of this city, which is as follows:

"My Dear Commander, I believe that the Grand Army of the Republic should inculcate principles of patriotism to the end that our free institutions may be perpetuated and the honor of our flag maintained at home and abroad, and that the pupils of our public schools be instructed on the subject of the late Civil War, its causes and effects. There has been quite a demand for speakers from the ranks of the G.A.R. on the part of the public schools for the proper celebration of Washington's, Lincoln's and Grant's birthdays, Memorial and Thanksgiving days, in a becoming manner by patriotic exercises, including vocal and instrumental music, quotations, Rotations and addresses. More and more the children of our cities are quite young, many without the least idea of the responsibilities of citizenship; hence the necessity of upholding and strengthening the hands of the school authorities in their heroic efforts to create true manly love of country and loyalty to the flag. I ask of the comrades of your post who can make this little sacrifice to good cause to have your hearty cooperation in this and all other respects."

N.J., will meet at their headquarters, No. 151 William-st., on Monday, May 31, at 8:00 a.m. and, after partaking of substantial luncheon, will proceed, under command of Colonel Henry H. Liebenau, to Greenwood Cemetery and decorate the grave of Colonel Abram S. Vosburgh, also the graves of Comrades Sergeant Charles F. Pearsall, Sergeant Stephen F. Egbert and Sergeant Francis B. Shelly. A committee of two comrades of the Vosburgh Veterans will also be sent to the burial places of Comrades William W. Dilks, former Police Superintendent, J. L. Tyson, A. L. Dixon, W. 4. The following details have been made: Captain Audrey, N.J., Sergeant George W. Wyckoff, orator of the day. Comrades are to wear dark clothes, with the Vosburgh veteran medal on the left lapel. The chairman of the Memorial Committee will be at headquarters, No. 151 William-st., on the morning of Decoration Day, Monday, May 31.

The next regular meeting of Abel Smith Post will be an open one at headquarters, Amphion Rooms, No. 41 Bedford-ave., Brooklyn, this evening at 8 o'clock sharp. Doors open at 7:30 o'clock. Police Commissioner James H. Bell, commander, and Adjutant John W. Haslam have issued invitations asking comrades to bring their friends. No tickets of admission will be necessary.

Joi and Peter Vosler with the medal of honor for twenty-five years honorable service in the post. The medals of sterling silver were presented by Commander Fred Leiser. Experiments have been made to see
if the number of rows of corn on cob
could not be increased with success.
The same method which was pursued
with corn is applicable to poultry
breeding. For example, one starts
with fowls which lay one hundred and
twenty eggs each in a year. Among
their descendants are some which lay
one hundred and fifty eggs per year,
and these are selected for breeding.
From these some are produced which
lay one hundred and seventy-fve eggs
per year, and from these, perhaps, the
two-hundred-egg-per-year hen is pro-
duced. The problem is not quite as
simple with fowls as with corn, for it
is necessary to breed the males, as we'll
as the females, year after year, from
prolific layers, in order to succeed. If
one looks after the breeding of the
females only. he may introduce on the
male side blood which is lacking in
prolifcacy, and thus check every at.
tempt at progress. 1t becomes neces-
sary, therefore, to breed the males
from hens which are varying in the
desired direction, and which show a
cumulated variability in that direc-
lion. It is just as essential that the
male should be from a hen which laid
one hundred and seventy-fve eggs and
whose mother laid one hundred and
fifty eggs, if the two-hundred-egg
bird is to be produced. Improvers of
laying fowls are too apt to forget this
and introduce males with little regard
to their breeding, and then wonder
why the prolifcacy OF the flock does
not increase, Reliable Poultry Jour
nal.

Weyler has cabled to Madrid in answer to dispatches from the Prime Minister that he is obliged for the moment to remain in Havana in order to have full control of the military operations in Santiago de Cuba, as cable dispatches from there and other reports by land can more easily reach him here than in Las Villas. They want him in Santiago de Cuba to share with them the responsibility for the campaign.

The destruction of Catalina de Guines, in Havana province, which I previously reported to THE SUN, was a great victory for the Cubans. In spite of the wire fences and deep ditches surrounding the town, the fifteen forts which sheltered the garrison, and the church and railroad depot, which were also fortified, the Cubans entered the place, after a fight of nine hours. The last struggle of the Spaniards was in a trench in the centre of the town, defended by 50 soldiers. It was taken in a hand-to-hand fight, and then the town burnt.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 21.-Two repre-
sentatives of the North American Trad
ing and Transportation company,
Messrs. P. B. Weare and Michael Cud-
ahy of Chicago, arrived here during
the day.


They came at the special request of
Secretary of War Alger, who desired
to confer with them in regard to the
question Of sending relief supplies to
the gold seekers in the Klondike coun-
try, should the investigation begun by
Captain Ray show such measures to
be necessary. Shortly after the arrival
in the city two gentlemen went to the
residence of Secretary Alger where they
remained in consultation with him the
greater part of the evening. Secretury
Alger said later that nothing final had
been determined upon and that nothing
would be until report had been re-
ceived from Captain Ray.

It was opened yesterday afternoon by Chemist Hamilton, who detailed the result of experiments on cadavers in Bellevue Hospital with great particularity. His testimony cannot be viewed in any other light than as extremely damaging to the accused, and this was shown by the nervousness and impatience of the counsel for the defense. He kept up a continual fire of objections and was on his feet all through the examination, which was one of the hottest legal engagements ever fought in the old Court House. The battle was at its fiercest when the District Attorney tried to elicit the fact from the witness that measurements taken of the deceased woman's arm proved she could not have fired the fatal shot herself. After long tilt, witness was allowed to answer the question as to how far the victim could possibly have held the weapon from her head, crooked her elbow and pulled the trigger. The reply was in the significant words, "six and a half inches."

Earlier in the examination he had stated the effect of a shot at this distance to be as follows:—"The skin surrounding bullet hole was covered with powder and smoke over an area of four inches in diameter. General Charles A. Dimon, a cartridge manufacturer, of Lowell, Mass., and manager of the United States Cartridge Co., was next called. Dover Association, which is 900, on Tuesday at Walnut-Grove Baptist church, in Hanover, is one of the largest Baptist bodies in the State. It was constituted in 1852 and at that time embraced all the territory now occupied by both the Dover and the Chickahominy. Subsequently, there was a division of the territory. At present all the white Baptist churches in Richmond and in the Peninsula, between the York and the James, except Hampton, a number in King William, Henrico, and Goochland, are with the Dover.

There are sixty-three of these churches, with seventy-four ordained ministers, with membership of nearly 1900, and Sunday-school attendance of 1920. The church property in the Dover Association is estimated to do worth $355,150; for salaries of ministers and other church expenses, $51,616 was given in 1896; for missions $13,703.39 was given, with miscellaneous and unclassified contributions, making a handsome total of $56,158 given to good causes by sixty-three churches.

ASSOCIATION OFFICERS.

The moderator of the association is Rev. J. D. Hutson, of Richmond, who has held his pastorate longer than any other minister in the body. It is thought that he will be reelected without opposition. Mr. Josiah Ryland, Jr., is the treasurer. Mr. Hutson has associated with him on his Executive Committee Rev. Walter Sydnor, Rev. W. W. Bowden, Rev. J. J. Ryland and Rev. W. H. Pitt.

The church in which the meetings are to be held is on historic ground. It is exactly seven and a half miles from Richmond. The shortest and pleasantest route is along the Mechanicsville turnpike to Mechanicsville, at which point the right-hand road is to be taken, and the church will be found about one and one-half miles further on. Only a mile or two away are the battle-fields of Mechanicsville, Ellerson's Mill, Gaines' Mill, and Cold Harbor. The neat building in which the association will gather was used as a hospital during the battles around Richmond, and many a gallant soldier suffered the loss of life or limb within its walls.

IN A BEAUTIFUL GROVE.

The church stands in a beautiful grove of oaks, and arrangements have been made for outdoor preaching. Visitors from a distance are expected, among them Dr. Charles J. Cooke, of Hollis, who makes a point to attend the Dover; Dr. Thames, of Danville, who will be down for a day or two; distinguished ministers from Norfolk, Petersburg, and elsewhere. It is not possible to forecast the probable procedure of a body so democratic as this, but so far as can be foreseen, the session is likely to be very harmonious. Nobody knows of any exciting issue likely to be made. It is thought probable that most of the time not devoted to the missionary, benevolent, and educational work of the denomination will be given to local interests.

Rev. J. C. Hillen, D. D., will preach the introductory sermon.

HOW TO GET OUT THERE.

Reduced rates have been secured for delegates who will travel by rail. Richmond is their nearest station. From Richmond delegates and visitors must either reach the church by private conveyance or they must take the bus from the Religious Herald Office on East Main street. This leaves Tuesday morning at 8:30 and returns that afternoon. It will leave the same place Wednesday and Thursday mornings at the same hour. The cost of the round trip is 20 cents.

The Committee on Entertainment publishes the following in the last Religious Herald. The best entertainment in the service of the Church and community is given, and cordial invitation is extended to delegates and representative brethren. The Church regrets that it cannot provide conveyances either from Richmond to the church or from the church to the homes of the people.

Rev. Charles H. Ryland is the pastor of the church.

Miners Complain Against the Injustice of Company Stores,

Clearfield, Pa., May 1.—THE legislative investigating committee met in the law library of the courthouse yesterday. A number of miners were examined. The company store seems to be their greatest grievance, and those on the witness stand denounced it as the greatest injustice with which they have to contend. The company to which Judge Dean belongs was denounced in especially severe terms. A number of miners testified that they were forced to deal at the company stores or lose their positions. One miner said he had been discharged for refusing to deal at these stores.

Mr. Hedding, superintendent of the Morrisdale Coal company, was the only operator present. He said his company did not discriminate against miners who did not deal at the company store. He said the company bought the best goods in the market and sold them as cheap as the same goods could be obtained elsewhere.

There is much suffering in this region on account of the destitution caused by lack of employment.

The first session in Scranton was not a success, but through no fault of the members, the subpoenas not having been served on witnesses. W. H. Storrs, assistant general coal agent of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western company, and General Superintendent W. A. May of the Hillside Coal and Iron company, the only witnesses, said there was no truth in the rumor that mine employees were in a destitute condition. The companies they represented had made no profit, they averred, for several years.

Wilkesbarre, Pa. Sept. 10.—Sheriff

Martin arrived home on the 3 o'clock

train from Hazleton. He was cool and
collected. He was met at the depot by
his legal adviser. The two got into a
carriage and drove to the court house
where they were closeted together for
some time. At first the sheriff refused

to say anything, but finally consented.
The sheriff was at first reluctant
to say whether he had given the command
to fire, but afterwards admitted
that he had. The sheriff's detailed
statement is as follows:
I heard, early this morning, that the
strikers were going to march in the
breaker at Latimer and compel the

men there to quit work. I resolved to
intercept them and if possible prevent
them from reaching the breaker. One

of my deputies told me that the strikers
would probably be heavily armed.
I got my deputies, 20 in number, to
meet at a certain place. They were all
armed. I told them to keep cool under
all circumstances.

The trouble began at 3 o'clock.
I met the marching column. I halted
them and read the proclamation. They
refused to pay any attention and
started to resume their march. I
called to the leader to stop. He ignored
my order. I then attempted to
arrest him. The strikers closed in on
me. They acted very viciously: kicking
me, knocking me down and trampling
upon me. I called upon my deputies
to aid me and they did so, but
were unable to accomplish much.

I realized that something had to be
done at once, or I should be killed.
I called to the deputies to discharge their
firearms into the air but it had no
effect whatever on the infuriated
foreigners, who used me more like wild
beasts than human beings. The strikers
then made a still bolder move and
endeavored to surround my entire
force of deputies. I fully realized that
the foreigners were a desperate lot and
valued life at a very small figure.
I then called upon the deputies to defend
themselves and shoot if they must to
protect their lives or to protect the
property they had been sent to guard
from being demolished.

The next second there were a few
scattered shots fired into the infuriated
foreigners and a moment later the entire
force of deputies discharged a
solid volley into the crowd. I hated to
give the command to shoot and was
awfully sorry that I was compelled to
do so and I was there to do my duty
and I did it as best I knew how. The
strikers were violating the laws of the
commonwealth and flatly refused to
obey the proclamation that I read to
them.

The scene after the shooting was
simply terrible and the entire crowd of
foreigners as soon as the volley had
been fired by my deputies turned and
started to retreat. They rushed off in
all directions as fast as they could,
taking as many of their dead and
wounded with them as they were able
to carry during their hurried retreat.
The excitement at the time was simply
terrible and I would not care to ever
go through another ordeal of the same
kind for fortune.

In another interview, Sheriff Martin
said he first met the marching miners at
West Hazleton. According to Martin's
story, when the strikers reached the line
of deputies he ordered them to halt and
disperse. One of the men said in broken
English: "Go to hell, you—" Martin's
men attempted to arrest the man who
made the remark, and, as he claims, was
fiercely assaulted by the man's friends.
Then the firing began. Mr. Martin was
asked during the interview:

"When you met the men were they on
company property or on the public road?"
He replied: "No, they were on the public
road."

"Had they up to that time committed
any overt act or acted otherwise than
peaceable?"

"No."

"Why then did you order the deputies
to fire?"

"I did not order the deputies to fire.
No one else did that. I gave no order."

"Were any of your men hurt?"

"One of my deputies was shot through
the arm."

Sheriff Martin, when he reached Wilkes
barre, was badly scared. Though he
claims to have been brutally ASSAULTED,
men saw he did not have a mark on his
person to show that he had been roughly
handled. All classes of citizens in this
city and county unite in condemning
Sheriff Martin's hasty action.

The Heroism of Duke Charles of Bavaria


In Theater Fire.


The bravery of battle is surpassed in the
quality and fiber of its intrepidity by the
courage which faces conflagration or a
wreck, because the battle fervor is helped
out by patriotism, esprit de corps and
other emotions which have a distinct
place in the soldier's heart. The great
charity bazaar fire at Paris, and particular
ly the heroic death there of the Duchess
d'Alencon, recalls brave exploit of this
lady's uncle, Duke Charles of Bavaria,
many years ago.


It was in 1823, and some sort of oper-
ational representation at the Residenz theater at Munich had attracted large and
brilliant audience. Duke Charles was seat
ed in the royal box. Suddenly an attend
ant rushed in and whispered excitedly:


"Your highness, the theater is on fire!
Make your escape before the panic breaks
out."


This alarming announcement did not
cause change of expression on the
PRINCE'S face. First satisfying himself by
word of inquiry that the stage was really
on fire, the prince rose, stepped calmly to
the front of the box and said to the audi
ence:


"I am informed that fire has broken
out on the stage. There is time enough
for you all to get out before the danger be-
comes imminent. The only thing that you
have to fear is panic. I urge you, there-
fore, to quit the hall in the most perfect
order, and give you my word that if you
do so you will all escape. To prove that I
mean what I say I shall now sit down
and shall not leave my seat until the last
one of the audience is out of the house."


Duke Charles then sat down as unmoved
as if the performance was to proceed. The
sight of his calmness treasured the audi
ence, and the people moved deliberately
out in an orderly manner; the flames burst
through the curtain to the proscenium;
the people looked at Duke Charles, who
still sat imperturbably in his place. No
one could make a cowardly rush in the
face of such an example.

emptied, no one being hurt. Duke Charles
was the last to go out. In another instant
the interior was all on fire, and the house
was completely destroyed. Youth Companion.

Bericht über die Stärke der Seemächte.

Ableben des parteilosen Abgeordneten von Saibingen. — Die Streiks des Hamburger Hafens. — Seine neueren Umbrüche belastet. — Seutz über die Abgeordneten treten im preußischen Landtage für die Polen in die Schranken. — Das neue Handelsgesetzbuch im Reichstage. — Eine gut erpartete Unterredung über die auswärtige Politik.

Berlin, 9. Februar. Seit drei Tagen beriefte heute der preußische Baron v. Buolzberg, daß der Kaiser dem Reichstage hier eigenhändig von ihm aufgelegte Berichte über die Stärke der Kriegsflotten Deutschlands, Frankreichs, Russlands, der See-Staaten und Japans zugeschickt habe, und daß er (der Baron) dem Kaiser im Namen des Hauses zu danken beabsichtigte. Die Mittheilung wurde durch Hochruf aufgenommen.

Abgeordneter v. Saibingen.

Karl Weber, Abgeordneter des Wahlbezirks von Arbing, an Lande des Ober-Binger Waldes, unweit Winningen, wo er seit Jahren in stiller Zurückgezogenheit lebte, im Alter von 84 Jahren aus dem Leben geschieden. Der Verstorbene war Königlicher Marineoffizier der Reserve und Oberlieutenant a. D. In seinen Jahren hat er am Pferde eine bedeutende Rolle gespielt; er gehörte zur persönlichen Umgebung des Königs Ludwig des Zweiten, dessenäubiger und Reisebegleiter auf den geheimnisvollen Reisen aus dem bayerischen Hochgebirge, nach der Schweiz zum Berner Bahnhof und nach Paris und Wien er war. Nach dem plötzlichen Tode seines königlichen Herrn hat sich Hr. v. Washington, der mit der Prinz Maria v. Wittelsbach genannt v. Heimaufen, vermählt war, ganz dem Leben zurückgezogen.

Ein Protest zur Beilegung der Streiks in Hamburg.

Man hofft jetzt begründete Hoffnung, daß es binnen kurzem gelingen wird, den Arbeiterstreiks in Hamburg ein Ende zu machen und die Ordnung wiederherzustellen. Die sozialdemokratischen Führer, welche sie der Leitung des Streiks vorgestanden hatten, sind nachgarbe zu der Polizei gekommen, daß eine weitere ungeliebte Haltung der Arbeiter auf ihr Konto geschrieben werden würde. Sie haben sich infolge dessen bemüht, die Arbeiter zu beruhigen. Die sozialdemokratischen Stadt-Abgeordneten Großme, Legien, Wolfenburg und v. Simon conferiren mit dem Senator Spöl, dem Chef der Abteilung für Handel und Gewerbe und Präsident der Deputation für Handel und Schifffahrt, in Hinblick auf die Wiederanstellung der Streiker an den Staatskais. Eine baldige Wiederanstellung dürfte den Arbeitern ein Ende machen. Nur die fremden Arbeiter, deren Anwesenheit die Streiker bitter hat, sind somit abgesehen. Zurück sind 300 Arbeiter noch zurückgeblieben.

Die Zahl der ausgegangenen Hafenarbeiter, welche nicht wieder zur Arbeit zurückgekehrt sind, weil ihre früheren Arbeitsplätze besetzt wurden, hat übrigens eine betrübliche Erinnerung erweckt. Von den Ausgegangenen sind bis jetzt in runder 300 bis 300 wieder angestellt worden. Bekanntlich hat die Streikleitung den Ausstand offiziell für beendet erklärt, nachdem die Mittel des Streikfonds erschöpft waren. Sie hat auch einen Geschäftsbericht über die von ihr vereinnahmten und herausgegebenen Gelder veröffentlicht. Dieselben belaufen sich auf die enorme Summe von 1,378,530 Mark.

Die Polenfrage im preußischen Landtage.

Während der gestrigen Debatte im preußischen Landtage über die Vertilgung für das Ministerium des Innern wurden mancherlei Fragen und Beantwortungen laut. Der Abgeordnete Robert Sasdel, Kaufmann mit politischer Grundschaft und Stadtrat in Posen, evangelisch, Richter und Vertreter des Stadtkreises Posen, führte Klage über den Beruf der deutschen Behörden, den Polen ihre Muttersprache zu nennen, und beklagte sich über den deutschen Kulturpessimismus. Strange as it may seem, no one among her many admirers had had the temerity to seek her hand. This may have been due to the fact that wholesome respect for the choleric temper of old Freeborn impelled them to keep their distance, but it was more probable that the spirit of reverence with which the fair Mildred usually inspired members of the opposite sex bade them recognize their own unworthiness.


At the time that I entered Freeborn's service the feud between Freeborn and Marquand was at its height. Marquand was a man of middle age and questionable practices. Year by year his once large fortune had grown smaller and smaller, and he was now striving desperately to regain all he had lost. He was an inveterate gambler, and his ranch house was the resort of half the gamesters in the county. Among the men in his employ were several Englishmen who, it was said, had certain dark pages in the history of their lives which it was to their best interests to conceal. They were not without future prospects, however, and night after night, when not engaged with the herds, they were to be found sitting around old Marquand's gaming table.


I had been on Freeborn's ranch about three months when the time arrived for a roundup. A new cause of dispute had lately arisen between Freeborn and Marquand, and I had been told to look for trouble.


One night, while I was sitting alone before our camp fire, awaiting the return of my companions, I fell to thinking of Mildred Freeborn. Since I had first met her she had interested me greatly. She had taken to me kindly, and often while I had been sitting with the men in the dining room of the ranch house she had sent Nettie, her servant, to me with the request that I should visit her in her little library. Although I was convinced that I occupied high place in her esteem, I was far from deceiving myself with the thought that I had inspired her with anything more than mere friendly regard. I was still under the influence of a former love affair, and though I admired and respected her I had felt no inclination to offer myself as a suitor.


I had found her an interesting study, however. In the course of our frequent conversations I had observed that she was dominated by a spirit of passionate unrest. The life she led on the plains had become irksome to her. She craved the social glamour and excitements of cities, which she had known only in the books she read. I had lived in the unknown country and was familiar with its customs and its sights. When she sought my company it was only that she might hear described those things she so fondly hoped one day to see.


There were times when I grew weary of her questioning, but her thirst for information was insatiate and she held me to my task.


During the last few days, however, her conduct had undergone a change. She had become more petulant in her manner, and now seemed as desirous of avoiding my society as she had formerly been anxious to seek it. As I lay beside the blazing sticks, striving to find some reason for her altered demeanor, my reverie was suddenly interrupted by the arrival of Tom Baxter, one of the cowboys who had been branding cattle during the afternoon.


"Wal, Dick," he drawled, as he seated himself carelessly beside me on the ground, "shows that thar coffee comin'? I'm hungry, an' thar's lot o' hard work ahead fer us all tonight."


"What's up—anything special?" I asked.


"Nope. I reckon thar's nothin' what yer might call special, exactly," he said slowly. "Still, a fellow never knows what's liable to happen when these here Marquand boys is round."


He paused, and as I glanced toward him I saw an expression of gravity steal slowly over his rugged features.


"Confound their blasted hides, anyhow I," he exclaimed impatiently. "I'm afeerd one of the pesky lot is brewin' a peck o' trouble fer our old man this night. Wimmen's funny lot—dog-gone 'em all, I say—an' ull bear more watchin' an' children will."


"What have women got to do with it, Tom?" I asked, in surprise.


"A regular howdy-do, that's what, as you'll find out afore this round-up's done, reckon," retorted Tom, disgustedly.


"Surely you don't mean—" I began.


"Will yer keep a secret if I tell it ter yer?" he demanded, as he eyed me curiously.


I looked at him questioning ly.


"Kin yer?"


"Yes."


"Wal, then, just keep yer eyes peeled fer trouble agin the sun goes down termorrer night. That gal o' Freeborn's is likely one, but fer all that she's preparin' to take the bit atween them glis'nen' teeth o' hern an' bolt her daddy's trail. One o' them Marquand boys—an' English lad named..."

Prosecute Dam Builders.


The Washington correspondent of the Albuquerque Democrat writes this paper:


As you have already seen the attorney general has been called upon by the Mexican minister to take cognizance of the contemplated wholesale scooping up of the waters of the Rio Grande by the big dam builders down at old Fort Selden.


The Mexican government claims that the Rio Grande is navigable for 125 miles above El Paso for rafts and flatboats, but we who know the sullen stream know that only the very lightest draught raft could float on its waters the greater part of the year. That any kind of craft can, brings the late secretary of the interior, Hoke Smith, and the English company under the process of the courts. The end is not yet and the fight may assume international proportions, for John Bull protects his own.


Hon. W. B. Childers, United States attorney, was seen at his office this morning, by a reporter for the Albuquerque Citizen, and was asked to give his views regarding the recent decision of the United States attorney general as to the construction of dams and reservoirs on the Rio Grande, and to a number of questions, Mr. Childers said:


"All I have to say about this matter is, that I understand, from instructions I have received from the department of justice, I shall take steps to procure an injunction if necessary to prevent the construction of dam in the Rio Grande river by the Rio Grande Dam and Irrigation Co., at point called Elephant Butte, about 125 miles above El Paso. It is held by the war department that the Rio Grande is a navigable stream up to El Paso and has been recognized by congress to be a navigable water at El Paso, and upon this the construction of the dam was illegal. The river and harbor act of 1890 prohibited the creation of any obstruction not affirmatively authorized by law, to the navigable capacity of any waters in respect to which the United States has jurisdiction, and made it a penal offense to so obstruct such water, and provided that it is alleged that this company proposes to irrigate all lands that could be reached from the dam and reservoir which it proposes to construct at this point, and that it proposes to use all the water in the river and prevent its natural flow, and that this would obstruct and interfere with navigation on the river below.


I am instructed to communicate with the company, and if it proceeds to construct this dam, to take such proceedings in court as may be necessary to prevent it. It will be entirely improper for me to express any opinion as to whether this action on the part of the government is proper or ill-advised. At least, it is one of those questions that it would be well to have the courts settle. I may add that the status of the Rio Grande in respect to the right to take water out of it from its source to its mouth raises many interesting questions. The people in this part of the country have been complaining for many years that, although they had priority of right in the use of the water of the Rio Grande, the people of Colorado have taken so much water out of the Rio Grande by dams and ditches, as to seriously reduce the amount of water available for the people of New Mexico, and to cause the stream to go dry in the summer time where it never was known to do so before. If this matter is brought into the courts, it may lead to some interesting decisions on this question, and it may prove beneficial also in directing attention to the interstate questions I have just mentioned."

Where now but a score of men are at work thousands will be employed and Kingman and Yuma will receive benefits to enumerate which would stagger the most sanguine inhabitant. Following on the heels of this great inter-national line would be built connection with the Utah Southern road and the coal field of Utah opened to the world's commerce. As railroad center there is no reason why Kingman should not have big smelting plants for the reduction of ores from every point of the compass. The congregation of ST. Andrew's Protestant Episcopal Church, of Richmond Staten Island, is the oldest in Greater New York, for it can trace a continuous unbroken organization for 236 years. After public services had been conducted regularly for forty eight years the parish was granted a charter by Queen Anne in 1709. The founders of the congregation came to Staten Island with the Huguenots that accompanied the Dutch Director Minuit, in 1624, and worshiped with them for some years, or until they removed to Wallabout Bocht, since corrupted into Wallabout.

In 1675 a little church was erected near where the Fresh Kills bridge now stands, and its ruins are remembered by persons yet living. At that time the Rev. John Miller, who had visited Staten Island, wrote: "There is a meeting-house at Richmond, Staten Island, of which DR. Bonrepos is the minister. There are forty English, forty four Dutch and thirty-six French families."

These English families were the ones from whom is descended the present congregation and through their blood was transmitted, not only to the laity but to the clergy of the parish, for DR. Charming Moore, for a long time its faithful pastor and afterward Bishop of Virginia, married into one of those original families, and his son, DR. David Moore, succeeded him in the rectorship.

As many of the Huguenots departed for more southerly locations, their services were discontinued, and the remaining ones joined with the Church of England people, who held regular weekly worship, with a clergyman, when one could be had, and when not, the service was read by layman. This organization was continued until December 13, 1709, when the parish became a legal body under a charter of that date granted by Queen Anne.

When the charter arrived, with it came the gift of a silver communion service from the sovereign consisting of chalice and paten, each engraved with the words, "Anne Regina." These pieces are still a part of the parish's altar service, and are used regularly at the celebration of the sacrament.

In June, 1712, came a grant of valuable lands on Staten Island to the parish from Queen Anne, and in the following year the first church was built, under the direction of the Rev. Eneas McKenzie, rector of the parish. This building was destroyed by fire.

The records of this old parish were well preserved until about thirty years ago, when a difference arose in the vestry as to the ownership of certain lands, which one faction claimed was included in the grant to the parish and the other said was not, when the records disappeared. Since then a portion of them returned, by some person unknown to the present rector, Dr. Thomas S. Yocum. The oldest entry they present reads, under date of August 9, 1852: "Daniel Penny, son of Charles Penny and Dorothy his wife, baptised."

The original grant to the parish is also in DR. Yocum's possession, but where the other records are remains a mystery.—New York Herald.

At a recent department store, several costly gold-handled and jeweled articles were scattered over the glass counter, and the obliging clerk to the fashionable shopper was endlessly answering to satisfy the whims of a daughter of wealth, who had every appearance of having been raised by unlimited means. She had a costly toothbrush in her hand and was pointing to other articles with it in dissatisfied way. "This is not small enough," she said, "and the hair is not fine enough."

"It is our very best kinds of goods," suggested the clerk half apologetically.

"Then you ought to get something better. Yes, really, you ought," exclaimed the vain customer. "I can't sell such a lousy toothbrush as that to my Kelly."

She examined the stock, with a series of skeptical air of impatience.

"Then you want toothbrushes for your dog?"

"Yes, of course I do, and I want something very soft and very dainty," replied the voting woman. And, after a pause, she added, with an affectionate air, "There isn't ANYTHING too nice for my Eve."

"Certainly not," responded the clerk, with cordial smile. "Here are some brushes of rare quality. Here is one with hair as soft as silk and a handle of solid gold." The girl handled the expensive trinket for a moment and, without asking the price, said, "That will DO. Have it sent with the other things, please. When this spoiled maiden's father gets a bill from the fashionable jeweler, he will doubtless be moved to emotion by the cost." One toothbrush for dog, $22.30.

It is no uncommon thing for shopkeepers in New York to be called upon to supply these articles for dogs, monkeys, birds and other domestic pets. "I am convinced," continued Judge Brad-
ley, "that the committee did not want Mr.
McCartney's testimony, and many of the
questions asked him were highly imperti-
nent, both in a legal and in an ordinary
sense. If 15 per cent of them in this and
the other cases had been refused answers,
the witnesses would have been justified in
declining to answer them.


Mr. McCartney was not advised by the
committee that answers to the quest-
ions were desired, and the committee allowed
Senator Allen to put the questions and
Senator Allen allowed them to stand as
his. If the defendant had been advised by
the committee that answers were desired
by the committee, he might in that event
have answered them, rather than face the
consequences of refusal to answer them.
It is clear to me that a witness before
such committee ought not to be ad-
judged guilty of contumacy until he
has, after being duly advised and warn-
ed by the committee, persisted in a refus-
al to answer a question put by the committee,
or by its authority."


Judge Bradley Concludes.


Judge Bradley said that it is true that a
member of committee of this kind has
the right to interrogate witness, but the
witness must, before he can become guilty
of contumacy, be advised that such a
question is that of the committee or of a
majority thereof. And, in conclusion, the
judge remarked that, inasmuch as Mr.
McCartney had not been examined by the
committee, but by Senator Allen, and in-
asmuch as he had not been advised that the
questions were those of the committee or
that answers were desired by the commit-
tee, and had not been warned by the com-
mittee of the consequences of refusal to
answer them, the motion for a verdict of
not guilty would have to be granted.


"Therefore, gentlemen of the jury," said
the court, turning to the twelve men, "good
and true, you will return a verdict of
not guilty."

She might disregard his beseeching glances, affect to misunderstand his signals and his uttered hints, might seek, in constant ministrations to her husband's wants and whims, to guard herself, and to forget these omens of nearing crisis. But she comprehended his designs; marked with a thrill, that was the opposite to pain, his chagrin at his failure, and the augmented restlessness of his mien, betokening perplexity and desire. What was to be the end of this pursuit, and her evasion of it, when her own heart was the tempter's strongest ally? She dared not hear him say that she was dear to him as he had long been to her. Knowing, as she did, that she ought to spurn him from her at the remotest approach to this theme, she was never able to say with an honest purpose that she was likely to do it. If she doubted his intentions, she doubted herself yet more.

"John," she called through the front window, "where are you going? what brought you here?"

"Mr. Edward told me to call for him at 4 o'clock, ma'am. I thought he had spoken to you about it," was the respectful rejoinder.

There was no immediate reply, and he checked his horses to inquire.

"Will I go back, ma'am?"

"No; go on."

She threw herself upon the back seat again, with throbbing pulses and feeling that she had spoken the sentence which was to decide her fate for time and for eternity. "Heaven help me to stand fast!" was the tongue essayed to say, and while the heart was melting into tenderness, and vibrating with expectation.

It lacked ten minutes of the appointed hour when they reached the office, but Edward stood upon the doorstep, hat and gloves on.

"It is good in you to submit so quietly to my meddling," he began, by the time he was seated. "But I have something to say to you, a story to tell which I can no longer keep. You must have seen, although you have seemed not to do so, how I have logged your steps for some weeks past, in the hope of stealing an opportunity for confession. I have sometimes ventured to believe that your woman's wit and woman's heart had penetrated my secret; that what entered so largely into my thoughts and motives, made up so much of my life, could not remain hidden from your eyes. I wanted to tell you of it long ago, dear Connie, but the recollection of what was due to another withheld me, while I was yet uncertain that my love was returned. I had so little reason for hope, although hope has never flagged—mine is of a sanguine nature, you know—that I hesitated to speak openly. Now that I can feel firm ground under my feet, my happiness is mixed with much alloy. I must either take from one who is a hopeless invalid the ablest and most lovely nurse that ever man had; condemn him, whose claim the world would declare to be superior to mine, to lone illness and sorrow, or consent to a season of dreary waiting before I can call my darling my own. Do you wonder that thoughts such as these have preyed upon my spirits; racked me with anxiety, even in the blessed hour of assurance that my devotion was not wasted?"
