It is gratifying to learn from Washington that certain information has reached the treasury department showing that the United States are rapidly recovering from their period of financial depression and that before the end of the year this country will surely be out of the woods not only as regards commercial enterprises, but also in the operations of the treasury. This is a circuitous method of saying that before the end of the year the treasury income will be equal to the treasury outgo. It is an indirect mode of saying what the great Dingley said directly at the Boston bean banquet, that his bill would produce too much revenue by and by.

One item of the certain information which has been received at the treasury department is that during the first half of the present month the treasury outgo exceeded the treasury income by $5,763,192. Another item is that the excess of outgo during the first six months of the fiscal year was $43,772,331.

Upon these two items of certain information is based the statement that "congress will be brought face to face with deficit of $45,000,000 in five months." Seeing that the deficit for the first half of the present month is about $1,000,000 greater than the average semimonthly deficit since the beginning of the fiscal year, it would seem to be nearer the mark to estimate the deficit for five months at $48,000,000. There doesn't seem to be much in these facts to support the opinion that the deficit is to be turned into surplus at an early day. During all the months of depression following the panic there was no such deficit as there has been during the last six months, and there is every indication that it will be as great this month as it was last. Thus far it has been at the rate of more than $115,000,000 a year, against $90,900,900 the worst year after the panic.

No doubt imports will increase to some extent after the stocks of anticipatory importations are exhausted. But it takes a financial Mark Tapley to come out strong on the basis of such figures as those of the present year to date.

The Chronicle would invite the attention of the republican brethren once more to the theory which they so stoutly maintained for some four years that by no possibility could the country ever become prosperous again until the treasury receipts should be made to exceed the treasury disbursements. They adhered stoutly to that theory to the end of the last democratic administration.

But now they seem to have lost it. They improve every opportunity to say not that prosperity is about to return, but that it has already returned. And while they repeat this endlessly they are forced to admit that the disbursements not only exceed the receipts, but exceed them more than at any time since the great war expenditures ceased.

It behooves them to reconcile what they claim to be the undeniable facts with the theory which they used as an excuse for not coming to the relief of the treasury three years ago. If they fail to do this they need not be surprised if the people reject some other theories of theirs. — Chicago

The curious superstition that there
is an ocean above the clouds is illus
trated by the following strange story,
by an old English writer: "One Sunday
the people Of a certain village we're com
ing out of church on a thick, cloudy
day, when they saw the anchor of a
ship hooked to one of the tombstones-
the cable, which was tightly stretched,
hanging down flum the air. The peo-
pie were astonished; and while they
were consulting about it, suddenly they
saw the rope move as though some one
labored to pull up the anchor. The an
chor, however, still held fast by the
stone, and a great noise was heard in
the air, like the shouting of sailors.
Presently a sailor was seen sliding
down the cable for the purpose Of un-
fixing the anchor. When he had just
loosened it the villagers seized hold of
him, and while in their hands he quick
ly died, just as though he had been
drowned. About an hour after, the
sailors above, hearing no more of their
comrade, cut the cable and sailed
away. In memory Of this extraordinary
event, the people of the village made
the hinges of the church doors out of
the iron of the anchor" 1t is further
stated that these hinges, 'are still to
be seen there;" a bit of evidence much
like Munchausen's rope wherewith he
ono climbed to the moor. If you
doubted the story, you were confronted
with the rope.


There is another queer tale about
this aerial ocean. "A merchant of Bris-
;ol," it is said, sset sail with his cargo
for ireland. Some time after, while
his family were at supper, a knife sud-
denly fell in. through a window, on the
table. When the merchant returned
and saw the knife, he declared it to be
his own, and said that on such a day, at
such an hour, while sailing in an un-
known part Of the sea-, he dropped the
knife overheard; and the day and the
hour were found to be exactly the time
when it fell through the window" All
of which was once implicitly believed
by many, and regarded as incontrovert-
ible proof of the existence of sea above
the sky. One is at a loss to conjecture
how that unknown part of the sea"
connected with the rest of it. A
physical geography showing this would
be no small curiosity.-Boston Post

Republican Election District Association officers have Joined an Independent Party.
The assembly of the Republican Election District Association officers in Durland's Riding academy last night was a remarkable demonstration of thorough political organization. Tammany Hall, which is wont to be cited as the perfection of political organizations, with favorable conditions, never got so many district workers together at one time. In sweltering heat, responded to the call of President Quigg, to attend a perfunctory business meeting last night.

There are nearly 5000 of these election district association officers and more could not have set into the big riding academy. All seats were filled and fully two thousand men stood without the hall. There were more than 5000 present.

The speakers platform was erected on the last side of the building. On it, besides President Quigg, were Postmaster Van Colt, Gen. Q. H. Coils, George R. Bidwell, Abraham Cruiber, Gen. James N. J. Varnum, Charles A. Hess, George B. Deane, James W. Perry, and Alexander I. Mason. Most of the district leaders were on the floor marshalling their men.

The meeting was called simply to instruct the officers of the election district associations regarding their duties in the revision of the rolls and the new enrolment which will take place on next Tuesday night. President Quigg proceeded immediately to the work in hand. He said:

SPEECH OF PRESIDENT QUIGG.

At the outset of what must be a memorable meeting, I will speak under the means that should be employed to put our organization on a footing that is as strong as it is successful. On your intelligence, your valor, your loyalty, and your devotion to the cause, the success of our party depends. I shall not conceal from you the fact that the great task which we are about to see engage us is a difficult one. But let us not deny that the desire to arouse in each of you, my fellow workers, has much to do with the calling of this great assembly. I thank you for this magnificent response to the summons of the President of your County Committee. This is a meeting of real live men, not of postal cards and petitions. Cheers! You represent the Republican sentiment of your neighborhoods or you are not representative men. I address YOU.

Nothing can be more certain than that the honest Republican is the backbone of our Government. Nothing can be more certain than that we possess in our election district associations the means that can be brought home to every man who is a Republican. Our meeting tonight shall be to impress each one of us with a true sense of his personal duty. We are all committed to spend our days and nights and all our energies in systematic work within the bounds of the law, not forgetting, but working, working, all the while, that the object of our meeting will be already won.

The Republican party is an organization, and it must be an organization. It has many aspects which must not be lost sight of. You must know that success for that examination depends upon the strict observance of the law. [Cheers.] That discipline will be exercised and that obedience exacted and the resultant success of the party may not be doubted. [More cheers.] If the seven organization officers in each election district work as ceaselessly from now until election day with full determination to gain recruits to the cause; if that spirit permeates the organization and dominates all the districts, in the heat of the battle, the Republican ticket is bound to win. [Applause.] In the history of parties in this city, so admirable an organization is now available to the honor and strength of the party. From the Battery to the Westchester border, no single election district is as well organized as our own association for the better enforcement of their principles. There never was a time so easy and so efficient for a party as there is now. I cannot say that it is as yet a perfect organization. Where it is weak or where it has fallen into incompetent hands, it must be made strong. It must be made so that it is as good now as it has ever been, from a knowledge which is at least as good as any other. We are strong in numbers, in discipline, in all that goes to make a good organization to any other in the country.

Nonetheless, if we can make it better and we CAN, it is our duty to do it, and to do it soon. The great virtue of the New York District is the universality with which it extends the reach and breadth of the city. Its other virtues are the spirit of independence which it permits and the invitation which it extends to everybody who is a Republican. But its great evil, and one for which we must strive, is the lack of that fairly correct condition in which rolls ought to be preserved. The population of the city constantly shifts and changes, and a roll which is fairly accurate to-day is bound, under the best of circumstances, to be deficient.

Quigg then proceeded to instruct the officers on the details of the revision of the rolls. He made silent references to the fact that, as the executive, he must be responsible for the accuracy of the rolls. This declaration of military authority was accepted with cheers and cries of "That's right!" His declaration that the name of every man who has ceased to be a Republican or who has joined the Democratic party must be stricken from the rolls was greeted with a roar of approval. The evident reference to Reunion was understood. Following this, upon the question of enrolling new members, President Quigg said:

You must permit every man to enroll who will subscribe to the pledge that he acted with the Republican party in the last election and that he intends to do so at the coming election. There must be no ifs or buts about the latter proposition. He must abide by the decision of the organization and not be permitted to join the Democratic party with the understanding that he will nominate a certain candidate or do other things which he desires. I want to say to any man who wishes to take the pledge with a mental reservation:

We want you to join us if you acted with us last year and intend to act with us at the next election. We want you if you come in fully prepared to accept the results of our primaries and our conventions. But if you do not mean to abide by such results and your only aim is to assist in controlling our primaries to further the interests of another organization to which you owe a true allegiance, you may not join; for you will have no business with us. It is a fraud that you should attempt it.

The question has already been raised of whether a man who has signed a petition for the nomination of a particular man should have his name on the rolls.
